articles.title: Stanford Research Open-Sources Memorilla, a Latent Memory Module for Frozen LLMs
articles.content: Stanford researchers have released Memorilla, an open-source memory system for LLMs. The Memorilla memory system reads a whole document collection and hands a frozen LLM just 16 memory tokens. On FactKG, a frozen Qwen3-8B scored 84.33% with Memorilla, against 80.43% with every document in context. It did that with 108x fewer document tokens. Code, training recipes and checkpoints are public under Apache 2.0. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension. TL;DR Size: 194M-parameter trainable memory module. It always outputs 16 memory tokens, whatever the collection size. The encoder (Qwen3-Embedding-4B) and decoder (Qwen3-8B) stay frozen. Runs on: Linux with CUDA GPUs and Python 3.11. The quickstart needs 1 GPU with 80 GB (recipes ran on H100 80GB). No quantized variants disclosed. Performance: Highest reported average across 8 benchmarks (49.68), top score on 5 of 8. Best: PersonaMem-v2 accuracy of 44.60%, versus 27.92% for full context. Worst: PubMedQA accuracy of 59.00%, versus 69.00% for LLMLingua-2. What is Memorilla? Memorilla is a memory module that turns a document collection into 16 vectors for a frozen LLM. The work comes from Jure Leskovec’s SNAP group, with co-authors from Toronto, Penn and MIT. A frozen LLM can only use what sits in its context window. Full-context prompting grows slower as history grows. Retrieval pastes the chunks most similar to the question, and can miss weaker clues. Memorilla takes a third route: it learns what each question needs from the whole store. How does Memorilla work? The pipeline has 3 steps: Encode once. A frozen Qwen3-Embedding-4B embeds each document a single time. New documents never force re-encoding of old ones. Read per question. 16 learned slots attend to the question and the full store. The module uses 2 cross-attention layers with 8 heads. Inject. The slots are projected into Qwen3-8B’s input embedding space and prepended to the question. Only the memory module trains: 194,123,776 parameters for the 8B decoder. Training runs in 3 stages. Stage 1 uses about 1.98M Wikipedia paraphrase-reconstruction examples. Stage 2 adds about 1.34M examples from 10 QA and summarization datasets. Stage 3 fine-tunes on all 8 benchmarks. The full recipe takes about 19 hours on 4 H100 GPUs. How does Memorilla perform on benchmarks? All baselines use the same frozen Qwen3-8B, per the paper’s main table. Scores are self-reported by the research team. FactKG: 84.33% accuracy, versus 80.43% full context and 80.38% MemoRAG. PersonaMem-v2: 44.60%, versus 30.90% for xRAG, the next best method. TriviaQA: 57.00 exact match, just ahead of MemoRAG at 56.60. LaMP-4 / LaMP-7: 18.15 and 48.37 ROUGE-L, both the best scores. Average: 49.68, versus 41.92 for xRAG, 40.75 for LLMLingua-2 and 38.02 for Mem0. Memorilla loses on 3 benchmarks. On PubMedQA it scores 59.00%, while LLMLingua-2 reaches 69.00%. Those abstracts total only 324 tokens, so compression has little to gain. MemoRAG leads on PersonalizationV4 (67.88% vs 66.65%) and NarrativeQA ROUGE-L (20.51 vs 19.31). MemoRAG used about 690x and 50x more document tokens there. Compression peaks on NarrativeQA: 16 tokens replace 67,385 document tokens, a 4,212x cut. As agent memory, 8 memory tokens lift a Qwen3-4B TextWorld agent from 18.6% to 24.2% average success. &&& How fast is Memorilla compared to full context? On 1 H100, Memorilla answers in 0.74 s at 512 documents (about 128K tokens). Full context slows from 0.75 s to 19.9 s, which is 27x slower. The memory module itself takes about 2 ms. An optional memory cache precomputes cross-attention keys and values. On 1 B200, a question then takes 8.1 ms at 1M documents and 33 ms at 4M. With torch.compile, the 1M case drops to 5.0 ms. The cache costs 80 GiB at 4M documents. How do you run Memorilla? Install with uv on Linux, then load MemoryVLLM.from_pretrained. The first run downloads about 25 GB of models. Checkpoints live at memorilla/Memorilla-Qwen3-8B as Stage 1, 2, 3, PV4 and PMv2 folders. Each checkpoint must run with the decoder it was trained with (evaluation docs). Custom data needs parquet files with collection_id, question, answer and documents columns. The research team also released PersonalizationV4: 149 synthetic users, 200 conversations each, under CC BY 4.0. Memorilla vs Mem0, MemoRAG and xRAG Benchmark scores come from Memorilla’s paper, which ran every baseline on the same Qwen3-8B. Licenses come from each project’s repository. Memorilla (paper)MemoRAG (repo)Mem0 (repo)xRAG (repo)ApproachLearned latent memory tokensMemory model guides retrievalExtracted text memories1-token RAG compression (paper)Doc tokens per query (geo. mean)167842121What the LLM reads16 soft memory embeddingsRetrieved textRetrieved memory text1 projected embeddingLicenseApache 2.0Apache 2.0Apache 2.0Not disclosedFactKG (Acc)84.3380.3872.7978.98PersonaMem-v2 (Acc)44.6028.7627.4830.90PubMedQA (Acc)59.0067.0024.0036.00NarrativeQA (ROUGE-L)19.3120.5113.8016.92Average, 8 benchmarks49.6847.52 (our calc.)38.0241.92 Key Takeaways 16 memory tokens replace whole document collections for a frozen Qwen3-8B. FactKG: 84.33% vs 80.43% full context, with 108x fewer tokens. Highest reported 8-benchmark average: 49.68. Weak spot: PubMedQA at 59.00% and fine-grained facts. Apache 2.0 code; 194M-parameter checkpoints on Hugging Face. Check out the paper, browse the GitHub repo, and download the checkpoints. articles.title: Cmpnd Releases dspy-wsp: Weight-Space Programming Comes to DSPy
articles.content: Cmpnd has released dspy-wsp, a prototype optimizer that brings weight-space programming to DSPy. Weight-space programming is a technique in which a frontier LLM reads another model’s weights and edits them directly. There are no gradients, no training loop and no fine-tuning dataset. dspy-wsp packages this as WeightSpace, an optimizer that plugs into any DSPy program and metric. In Cmpnd’s tests, about $5 to $10 of GPT-6-Astra calls improved every decision model they tried. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension. TL;DR What it is: A DSPy optimizer (WeightSpace) where a writer LLM edits a student model’s weights. MIT license, pip install dspy-wsp, needs DSPy 3.5. Size: Tested on open decision models from 0.6B to 9B parameters. One 25-pass run edited a single layer or head. Runs on: One Mac for all experiments. 2B models used about 6 GB of memory. d1-omni-600M needs 4 GB or more (Mac or GPU). Performance: WeightSpace alone added 1.9 to 16.1 points on Typed Decisions. With ReAnchor, gains were 6.5 to 20.0 points. Best: d1-omni-600M rose from 50.9% to 69.1% (+18.3) with WeightSpace + ReAnchor. Worst: Clef-Flash (9B) gained only +1.9 from WeightSpace alone. With the original paper’s stricter rule, d1-omni-600M gained just +2.8. Bottom line: Best: a cheap, gradient-free edit that ships as a small, verifiable patch. Worst: very experimental, slow (78 to 167 minutes per run) and weakest on larger models. What is weight-space programming? Weight-space programming (WSP) treats a neural network’s weights as a program that can be read and rewritten. The idea comes from MIT research: Sparks of Weight-Space Programming. A frontier model (the research team used GPT-6-Astra) looks at weight tensors, reasons about what each part computes, and changes them to match a goal written in plain English. The research team stresses that WSP names an emerging capability, not a fixed method. Gradients were banned in their experiments, but the concept does not rule them out. How is it different from fine-tuning or prompt optimization? It helps to compare the 3 levers developers usually pull: Prompt optimization (DSPy’s MIPROv2, GEPA) edits text: instructions and examples. The model’s weights never change. Fine-tuning (DSPy’s BootstrapFinetune, used inside BetterTogether) changes weights with gradient descent. It needs training data, a training loop and usually a GPU. Weight-space programming changes weights by reasoning. The editor forms a hypothesis (“these neurons over-score option B”), writes code to patch them, and checks the result with a few forward passes. The research post frames WSP as the next step after using LLMs to optimize text artifacts. Earlier work let LLMs hill-climb on prompts, harnesses and training code. Weights were left to Adam or to trained weight-generating networks. WSP argues LLM reasoning can now reach the weights directly. What did the original research show? The MIT team ran 9 experiments. Several are striking: Reading weights: Astra named the correct game (Breakout, Pong, Pac-Man, Freeway) for 4 PPO policy networks from weights alone. Fixing a broken policy: A Kinetix car-on-ramp policy failed all 256 episodes. One edit to 3.5% of its weights made it succeed in all 1,024 test episodes. Writing from zero: On MinAtar Breakout, a zero-initialized network written in 1 shot scored 517.4. PPO reached 25.3 after 500M steps. Fixing an LLM: Qwen3.5-0.8B looped on math problems. Astra traced the issue to MLP layers 15 and 19 and changed 131,072 weights (0.016% of the model). With 50 forward passes, MATH-500 rose from 7.9% to 48.1% and GSM8K from 13.8% to 67.1%. The research also shows limits. On Gemma 3 270M, edits moved MATH-500 from 6.8% to between 7.0% and 7.7%. The research team did not count that as a real gain. Editing can remove an obstacle, but it could not add a missing ability. How does dspy-wsp work? dspy-wsp turns that research loop into a standard DSPy optimizer. The GitHub Repo describes 3 actors: The student: the small model your DSPy program runs on. Its weights load into a local Python process. The writer: a frontier LLM, recommended as gpt-6-astra at maximum reasoning effort. The sandbox: a kernel where the writer runs code. macOS uses built-in sandbox-exec; Linux uses bubblewrap. The writer works in turns. Each turn has a short explanation, then 1 code block. That block is either: a Python block that reads or edits weights inside the sandbox, or a forward block that runs your DSPy program on practice examples. Forward passes come from a fixed budget (max_passes=25 in the tests). When the budget runs out, the writer’s best edit becomes the patch. A hidden validation set then compares original and edited weights on the same examples and seeds. What data does the writer see? The repo is explicit about data separation: trainset is the writer’s practice set. holdout moves a fraction (0.25 in the example) of training data into a check set. The writer can score edits on it but never sees the examples. valset stays hidden and runs once at the end. Metrics can return dspy.Prediction(score=..., feedback=...). The feedback text is visible to the writer. What did the writer actually change? The results write-up lists every edit. The edits are small and targeted: ModelTensor editedScopeTimeWriter costd1-omni-600Mhead.scorer.1.weight (+ bias, scorer.3.weight)112,640 of 1,048,576 entries, plus 22078 min$7.63NanoJev (Qwen3-0.6B)scalar.weight1,024 entries167 min$6.92d1-2Blayers.23.feed_forward.w2.weightAll 15.7M entries, rank-9 change83 min$5.42 d1-2B has no decision head, so the writer edited its backbone at layer 23. On d1-omni-600M, the writer rewrote part of the decision head’s scorer. What does the code look like? The Repo example triages support tickets. The signature uses only decision-type outputs: Copy CodeCopiedUse a different Browserimport dspy from typing import Literal from dspy_wsp import WeightSpace, load_decision_backend class Triage(dspy.Signature): """Triage a support ticket.""" ticket: str = dspy.InputField() urgent: bool = dspy.OutputField(desc="Does this ticket need a reply today?") team: Literal["billing", "technical", "account"] = dspy.OutputField(desc="Which team should handle it?") backend = load_decision_backend("d1") # d1-omni-600M optimizer = WeightSpace( metric=metric, writer_lm=dspy.LM("openai/gpt-6-astra", model_type="responses", reasoning_effort="max"), backend=backend, max_passes=25, holdout=0.25, run_dir="runs/triage", ) compiled = optimizer.compile(dspy.Predict(Triage), trainset=train, valset=test) compiled(ticket="I was charged twice this month.") # runs on the edited weights After compile, the program calls the edited local model instead of a hosted API. compiled.wsp_patch.summary() shows what changed. articles.summary: Cmpnd가 공개한 dspy-wsp는 다른 모델의 가중치를 LLM이 직접 수정하는 가중치 공간 프로그래밍을 DSPy에 연결한 실험적 최적화 도구다. 경사 계산이나 미세조정 데이터셋 없이 동작하며, 회사 측은 6억~90억 매개변수 의사결정 모델 실험에서 WeightSpace 단독으로 1.9~16.1점의 성능 향상을 보고했다. 다만 원 논문의 더 엄격한 평가 규칙에서는 특정 모델의 향상이 2.8점에 그쳤고, 실행당 78~167분이 걸려 효과와 효율을 일반화하기 어렵다. MIT 라이선스로 제공되는 프로토타입으로, 작은 가중치 패치만으로 모델 동작을 바꾸는 새로운 최적화 가능성을 제시한다.

articles.title: Run Native DLA Inference in Python on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin Using cuDLA
articles.content: AI applications at the edge often need to run multiple neural networks within limited compute and power budgets. NVIDIA Deep Learning Accelerator (DLA)...AI applications at the edge often need to run multiple neural networks within limited compute and power budgets. NVIDIA Deep Learning Accelerator (DLA) platforms provide dedicated hardware for deep learning inference. On NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, DLA executes supported neural network operations, allowing applications to offload inference work from the GPU. This can improve power efficiency and leave… Source
articles.summary: NVIDIA는 Jetson AGX Orin에서 cuDLA를 이용해 Python으로 네이티브 DLA 추론을 실행하는 방법을 소개했다. DLA는 지원되는 신경망 연산을 전용 하드웨어에서 처리해 GPU의 추론 부담을 덜어준다. 연산 자원과 전력이 제한된 엣지 환경에서 여러 신경망을 운영할 때 전력 효율 개선에 도움이 될 수 있지만, 제공된 자료에는 지원 연산 범위나 정량적 성능 비교가 없다.

articles.title: Adapt Human Motion for Robots with NVIDIA SOMA Retargeter
articles.content: Human motion offers roboticists a great starting point for teaching humanoid robots how to move. A human demonstration captures the coordination and timing...Human motion offers roboticists a great starting point for teaching humanoid robots how to move. A human demonstration captures the coordination and timing behind natural movement, from everyday actions to complex tasks. But a robot cannot simply copy the same joint motion from a human. Its proportions, joint structure, and range of motion are different, so the movement needs to be adapted to fit… Source
articles.summary: NVIDIA는 사람의 움직임을 로봇에 맞게 변환하는 SOMA Retargeter를 소개했다. 사람의 시연에는 동작의 협응과 타이밍 정보가 담겨 있지만, 로봇은 신체 비율과 관절 구조, 가동 범위가 달라 그대로 복사할 수 없다. 이 도구는 이러한 차이에 맞춰 동작을 조정하는 문제를 다루며, 휴머노이드 동작 학습에 인간 시연을 활용하는 데 의미가 있다. 제공된 발췌에는 구체적인 변환 알고리즘이나 실제 로봇 성능 평가가 포함되지 않았다.

articles.title: Vercel Releases UI SDK: 50+ UI Behaviors for AI Coding Agents
articles.content: Vercel Labs has released UI SDK, an open-source beta library of interface behaviors built for coding agents. Vercel UI SDK is a headless library that ships behaviors, not finished components. Agents combine those behaviors into accessible components for React, Vue, Svelte, Solid and Web Components. You can check the deployment options and specs here through our GPULeaderboard.com chrome extension. TL;DR Size: 50+ behaviors, 51 component modules in the repo, 6 npm packages at 0.1.0-beta.1 Runs on: Any modern browser, no GPU. React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+, Solid 2 RC, or plain Web Components Performance: In Vercel’s own test, an agent used 69% fewer tool calls on a settings task Best: Task time fell 61%, from 41 s to 16 s, with the agent bridge (self-reported) Worst: That benchmark covers 1 task and 3 runs, and beta APIs may still change What is Vercel UI SDK? UI SDK is a library of UI behaviors from Vercel Labs that agents assemble into components. The README lists keyboard navigation, focus, selection, dismissal, popups, drag and drop, and the ARIA they need. All of it lives in @ui-sdk/core. Thin adapters render it in each framework. The project site explains the idea with a Select. You do not hand the agent a finished Select. You hand it a popup, a selection model and typeahead. Those same parts can produce an autocomplete, a combobox, or a component nobody has designed yet. How does UI SDK work? Components start as primitives defined with definePrimitive. A primitive declares state, an API and slots. Slots attach attributes, events and behaviors to DOM parts. The README example builds a search field with createFocusRecovery. Its Clear button appears only when there is text. Each framework then renders the primitive with createParts. The README says the parts are the same in all 5 adapters. So 1 behavior definition can serve a React app and a Svelte app. Which behaviors ship? Behaviors shown on ui-sdk.dev include: createRovingFocus: arrow keys move through a list with 1 Tab stop createTypeahead: type a few letters to jump to an item createPopup: opens next to its trigger and stays on screen createSelection: select 1 or many, with Shift and Ctrl createReorder, createResize, createViewport and createVirtualizer The docs group behaviors into 10 categories, from Focus and Keys to Canvas. Prebuilt components include Select, Combobox, Date Picker, Menu, Tree and Color Picker. How do agents learn it? Setup is a prompt you paste into your agent. It installs the packages and adds a note to AGENTS.md. That note points the agent to the ui-sdk skill and to llms.txt inside the package docs. The skill installs with npx skills add vercel-labs/ui --skill ui-sdk. Pages without a build step can load web.js and web.css from ui-sdk.dev, per the skill listing. && Can agents operate the UI directly? Yes, the agent docs describe a bridge created with createAgent() before the page renders. agent.snapshot() lists components, their state and available actions. agent.act() runs an action, such as renaming a project with setValue. Apps can pass an allow callback to approve or refuse actions. Change callbacks receive source: "agent" and can cancel the change. Tools can also be registered with supported browsers through WebMCP. UI SDK benchmark: agent bridge vs browser tools Vercel compared its bridge against browser tools on 1 project-settings task. The agent renamed a project, updated members and notification settings, then saved. Both agents used Sonnet through Claude Code, with the same task and system prompt. Figures are medians of 3 runs. MetricBrowser toolsUI SDK + bridgeChangeTool calls165-69%Text read (characters)39.8k6.8k-83%Time41 s16 s-61%Cost$0.073$0.032-56% Treat these as directional. The sample is 1 task, and the browser-tools run used a different component library. Vercel does not name the Sonnet version. Deployment and availability All 6 packages are on npm at 0.1.0-beta.1, published November 12, 2026, under Apache-2.0. Install with npm install @ui-sdk/react @ui-sdk/core, swapping the adapter per framework. Peer requirements are strict: React 19+, Vue 3.5+, Svelte 5.33+ and Solid 2.0.0-rc.14+. An optional web.css file gives components a default look. How does UI SDK compare with Radix, React Aria, Base UI and Ark UI? MetricsUI SDKRadix PrimitivesReact Aria ComponentsBase UIArk UIModelBehaviors composed by agentsUnstyled componentsHooks and componentsUnstyled componentsComponents on Zag.js state machinesFrameworksReact, Vue, Svelte, Solid, Web ComponentsReactReactReactReact, Vue, Solid, SvelteLicenseApache-2.0MITApache-2.0MITMITLatest npm version0.1.0-beta.11.8.11.22.11.9.05.40.0React peer range19+16.8 to 1916.8 to 1917 to 1918+Agent skill and runtime bridgeYes (skill, llms.txt, createAgent, WebMCP)Not disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosedNot disclosed Versions and peer ranges are from npm as of November 13, 2026. React Aria hooks and Ark UI’s Zag.js machines already separate behavior from markup. UI SDK’s difference is the agent layer: a skill, bundled llms.txt and a runtime bridge Key Takeaways 50+ behaviors, 1 core, 5 framework adapters. Agents compose components from behaviors, not templates. createAgent lets agents act on UI state without screenshots. Self-reported: 61% faster and 56% cheaper on 1 task. Beta at 0.1.0-beta.1, with React 19 as the minimum. Check out the GitHub repo, docs and npm package. articles.title: "생성형 AI로 세무사시험 수석 합격했다"…당사자 부정행위 인정하고 자수
articles.content:
제63회 세무사시험 수석 합격 논란의 당사자가 생성형 인공지능(AI)과 전자기기를 이용해 시험에서 부정행위를 했다고 공개적으로 인정했다. 세무사 1차와 2차 시험뿐 아니라 공인회계사 1차 시험에서도 같은 방식으로 부정행위를 저질렀다고 밝혀 전문자격시험의 공정성과 AI를 악용한 부정행위 방지 대책에 대한 논란이 커질 것으로 보인다.

온라인에서 '세무냥이'라는 이름으로 활동해 온 한ㅇㅇ 씨는 15일, 이돈호 변호사의 유튜브 채널에 공개된 영상에 출연해 자신의 부정행위 사실을 인정하고 사과했다. 한 씨는 영상을 통해 “저는 세무사 시험에서 부정행위를 했습니다. 제 잘못으로 많은 분들께 피해를 드린 점 진심으로 사과드립니다”라며 “제가 한 일을 모두 자수서에 써서 서울경찰청에 제출했다”고 밝혔다.

그는 세무사 1·2차 시험에서 전자기기와 생성형 AI를 이용해 부정행위를 했다고 인정했다. 이어 공인회계사 1차 시험에서도 같은 방식으로 부정행위를 했으며, 합격 수기와 언론 인터뷰에서 사실과 다른 설명을 했다고 말했다. 부정행위 의혹이 제기된 이후에도 이를 부인했던 사실에 대해서도 사과했다.

초소형 카메라로 문제 촬영…생성형 AI로 답변 확인했다고 진술

한 씨는 영상에서 부정행위에 사용한 방법도 설명했다. 그는 “초소형 카메라를 이용해 시험 문제를 찍고 AI로 전송해서 스마트폰으로 답을 확인하는 방법으로 부정행위를 저질렀다”고 말했다. 이는 시험장에 반입한 전자기기로 문제를 촬영하고 생성형 AI를 활용해 답변을 확인했다는 당사자의 진술이다.

한 씨는 사용했던 장비 가운데 일부는 파손된 상태이며, 남아 있는 증거자료를 수사기관에 제출할 예정이라고 밝혔다. 제출할 자료의 목록은 이미 자수서와 함께 전달했다고 설명했다. 다만 실제 부정행위가 이뤄진 구체적인 과정과 사용된 AI 서비스, 장비의 종류, 시험 감독 체계를 어떻게 통과했는지 등은 영상에서 상세히 공개되지 않았다. 관련 사실관계는 향후 수사를 통해 확인돼야 한다.

한 씨는 자신의 수석 합격이 정당한 노력으로 얻은 결과가 아니라고 인정했다. 그는 부정행위를 저지른 배경에 대해 직장 퇴사 이후 자영업을 운영하는 과정에서 경제적 어려움을 겪었고, 전문직 시험을 통해 다시 성과를 얻고 싶었다고 설명했다.

30대에 시험 준비를 시작하면서 수험 기간이 길어질 수 있다는 불안감이 컸고, 결국 부정행위를 선택했다고 말했다. 그러면서도 어떠한 개인적 사정으로도 부정행위가 정당화될 수 없다고 강조했다. 특히 지난 10월 28일 세무사시험 수석 합격 사실을 확인했을 당시 차석 합격자에게 미안한 마음이 들었다고 밝혔다.

한 씨는 자신의 부정행위로 성실하게 시험을 준비한 수험생과 다른 합격자들이 피해를 입었다며 사과했다. 현직 세무사와 시험 관계자, 자신을 응원했던 가족과 지인들에게도 사죄의 뜻을 전했다. 의혹이 제기된 뒤 언론 인터뷰에서 부정행위를 부인한 이유에 대해서는 갑작스러운 취재와 비판에 당황했고, 당시에는 사실을 숨기려는 생각이 있었다고 설명했다.

이후 자신의 행동에 책임을 져야 한다고 판단해 자수하게 됐다는 입장이다.

한 씨는 향후 조사와 수사에 성실하게 협조하겠다고 밝혔다. 그는 부정행위를 계획하고 실행한 과정뿐 아니라 사전에 준비하고 연습한 내용까지 수사기관에 설명하겠다고 말했다. 또한 세무사시험을 비롯한 각종 자격시험과 대학수학능력시험 등에서 유사한 부정행위가 발생하지 않도록 필요한 확인과 예방 조치에도 협조하겠다는 뜻을 밝혔다.

영상에 함께 출연한 이돈호 변호사 역시 수사기관과 시험 주관기관이 요청할 경우 부정행위 방법을 사실대로 설명하겠다고 말했다.

이번 사건은 생성형 AI가 전문자격시험의 공정성에 미칠 수 있는 새로운 위험을 보여준다. 기존 시험 부정행위가 외부인과의 통신이나 사전에 저장한 자료의 열람 등에 의존했다면, 생성형 AI를 악용하는 경우 시험 문제를 외부로 전달하고 AI가 생성한 답변을 확인하는 방식으로 부정행위가 이뤄질 수 있기 때문이다.

특히 전문자격시험은 합격자의 전문성과 직업적 신뢰를 공적으로 인정하는 제도인 만큼, 전자기기 반입 통제와 시험장 감독 방식이 새로운 기술 환경에 적절하게 대응하고 있는지 점검할 필요성이 제기된다.

다만 현재까지 공개된 내용은 한 씨가 영상에서 직접 밝힌 진술을 중심으로 한 것이다. 실제 부정행위의 범위와 방식, 관련 법령 위반 여부, 합격 처리에 미치는 영향 등은 수사기관과 시험 주관기관의 조사 및 판단을 통해 확정될 사안이다.

한편, 이번 입장 발표 영상은 15일 이돈호 변호사의 공식 유튜브 채널에 '세무사시험 수석 논란 당사자, AI 부정행위 자수했습니다'라는 제목으로 공개됐다. 약 14분 분량의 영상에는 한 씨의 사과와 부정행위 인정, 자수 경위, 수사 협조 계획 등이 담겼다.(아래 영상)
articles.summary: 제63회 세무사시험 수석 합격 논란의 당사자가 생성형 AI와 전자기기를 이용한 부정행위를 공개적으로 인정하고 자수서를 제출했다고 밝혔다. 본인 진술에 따르면 세무사 1·2차와 공인회계사 1차 시험에서 문제를 외부로 전달해 AI 답변을 확인하는 방식을 사용했다. 이번 사안은 생성형 AI 악용이 전문자격시험의 공정성과 전자기기 통제 체계에 새로운 위험을 줄 수 있음을 보여준다. 실제 실행 과정과 사용 서비스, 관련 증거는 향후 수사를 통해 확인돼야 하므로 시험 결과를 AI의 독립적인 문제 해결 능력으로 해석해서는 안 된다.

articles.summary: 테크크런치는 NVIDIA 보안 책임자가 8월에 조용히 회사를 떠났으며, 젠슨 황의 퇴진을 둘러싼 관계 중에는 중국으로의 칩 유출이 의심되는 기업 임원과의 관계도 있다고 보도했다. 기사에 인용된 전직 정보요원은 일상적인 대화를 통한 정보 유출을 일반 기업 보안팀이 포착하기 어렵다고 지적했다. AI 반도체 기업의 보안이 기술적 통제뿐 아니라 인적 관계와 정보 취급까지 포함해야 한다는 쟁점이지만, 제공된 자료만으로 실제 유출이나 위법성을 확정할 수는 없다.

articles.title: Yang-Mills, OpenAI proof, and the mass gap problem
articles.content:
A few days ago, OpenAI made an announcement aboutthe existence of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) and a unified completion of the Standard Model of particle physics. It sounds like a physics problem but this is actually the first half of theYang-Mills existence and mass gapproblem, one of the seven1-million $ questionsfrom the Clay Institute.

After Navier-Stokes a few weeks ago, my first thought was, OpenAI did it again?

Actually, not quite...yet.

As usual, to share their results with the world, they produced a huge manuscript (1147 pages !) along with a proof verified in Lean, a programming language in which a computer checks every single logical step of a mathematical proof. But Lean is not enough:we need to make sure that what the proof is about is really the problem mathematicians and physicists are interested in. A computer can check that a proof is correct, but not that the definitions written in the code mean what we think they mean.

For this, OpenAI called a special group to examine their proof. Andthe group just released its first assessment. To understand what is at stake, let me walk you through the Yang-Mills problem, its link to the strong nuclear force, and whether all of this matters for what happens inside particle accelerators.

As its name indicates, quantum field theory is about applying the principles of quantum mechanics to fields, like the electromagnetic field. Quantum mechanics is usually well defined when we are dealing with a finite number of degrees of freedom, like a bunch of point particles each having a position and a velocity. But with fields, which have a value at every point of continuous space, things get finicky.

You may have heard about thepath integralapproach to quantum mechanics, a beautiful idea due to Richard Feynman. The idea involves computing a giant integral over all the trajectories a particle can follow.

It might sound scary, but with a finite number of particles, we have ways to make this rigorous and well defined by taking careful limits. But applying the same idea to fields is complicated.

For a field, the "trajectories" are all the possible configurations of the field in space and time. Schematically, if A denotes our field andS[A]S[A]S[A]its action (the quantity that encodes the laws of the classical theory), the path integral reads

Z=∫DAeiS[A]/ℏZ = \int \mathcal{D}A \; e^{\,i S[A]/\hbar}Z=∫DAeiS[A]/ℏ

where the strange symbolDA\mathcal{D}ADAmeans "integrate over all possible field configurations" (similar to your familiardxdxdxin ordinary integrals.) Indeed, with fields existing everywhere in space, the field path integral involves an infinite number of integrals (one for each point of space!), and the path integral becomes generally ill-defined: there is no proper mathematical meaning forDA\mathcal{D}ADA, and divergences appear.

Still, that doesn't stop physicists from writing and manipulating them, in particular to define a certain type of objects calledcorrelation functions:

⟨O(x)O(y)⟩=1Z∫DAO(x)O(y)eiS[A]/ℏ\langle O(x)\, O(y) \rangle = \frac{1}{Z}\int \mathcal{D}A \; O(x)\, O(y)\; e^{\,i S[A]/\hbar}⟨O(x)O(y)⟩=Z1​∫DAO(x)O(y)eiS[A]/ℏ

where O is some quantity built from the field, at points x and y. These correlation functions essentially represent what we can observe experimentally, say in particle accelerators. And to see how physicists escape the ill-definedness problem, let's have a look at the quantum side of Maxwell's electromagnetism.

Let's start withpure electromagnetism, when no matter is present. This is the easy case, because the nasty path integrals can then be shown to be computable and well defined...But the resulting theory is not very interesting! This is because it only contains photons (the particle associated with electromagnetism), and they don't interact with each other. Pure electromagnetism is a theory of free photons moving in space, and passing past each other as if they were alone.

Now add matter, for instance electrons. We can write the path integral that describes the coupling of electromagnetism and electrons. The theory is supposed to be way more interesting because photons provide in principle a mean for electrons to interact...butthis time the big path integral it is not well defined. So the correlation functions are in theory meaningless.

The good news is that physicists found a way around, called theperturbative expansion.

The so-called coupling between electromagnetism and matter (it measures how strongly they interact, and is related to the famous fine-structure constantα≈1/137\alpha \approx 1/137α≈1/137) is weak enough, at least at large distances, that we can formally expand the ill-defined integrals in powers of this coupling, and truncate this expansion to a finite number of terms that we can actually compute. To show you the idea with a simple numerical integral, imagine you had to compute

I(α)=∫−∞+∞e−x2−αx4dxI(\alpha) = \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-x^2 - \alpha x^4}\, dxI(α)=∫−∞+∞​e−x2−αx4dx

then you realize that you can expande−αx4e^{- \alpha x^4}e−αx4in power series, which you can truncate to get integrals that are easier to compute

I(α)≈∫−∞+∞e−x2(1−αx4+α22x8+…)dxI(\alpha) \approx \int_{-\infty}^{+\infty} e^{-x^2} \left(1 - \alpha x^4 + \frac{\alpha^2}{2} x^8 + \dots\right) dxI(α)≈∫−∞+∞​e−x2(1−αx4+2α2​x8+…)dx

With the perturbative approach, each term of the expansion becomes symbolized by one of the famous "Feynman diagrams" that you probably have seen.

Along the way, infinities do show up, but physicists learned to absorb them in a systematic way, a procedure calledrenormalization. And the results of doing this are surprisingly accurate!

Even if the whole perturbation procedure seems crude, the numbers we find this way are in great agreement with particle physics experiments.This is even a big understatement: for the magnetic moment of the electron, theory and experiment agree to about one part in a trillion!!

In this resulting theory calledQuantum Electrodynamics (QED), we can compute interactions between photons and matter particles, and the fact that the photon is massless translates into the fact that electromagnetism is "long range", with forces decreasing as the inverse square of the distance,1/r21/r^21/r2, which we know from macroscopic experiments.

That being said, we know the perturbative expansion trick has its limits. First, if you tried to sum all the terms of the expansion instead of truncating it, the sum is believed to diverge: only the first terms are useful. Second, in QED the coupling slowly grows as you look at shorter distances (higher energies), and at some point the expansion would stop making sense. But in practice, this limit is so far away (at energies absurdly beyond anything reachable) that physicists don't care much, especially since QED gets absorbed into a bigger theory long before that.

The theory is "effective" even if not rigorous.Is there a way to define a rigorous version of QED (electromagnetism + matter)? Probably not! Numerical evidence suggests that if you try, the interactions disappear and you end up with a boring free theory.

Now what about the other forces?

Since things worked well enough for electromagnetism, physicists tried to apply the same recipe to the other forces, like the weak nuclear force (responsible for some types of radioactivity), or the strong nuclear force, which holds quarks together inside protons and neutrons, and, indirectly, protons and neutrons together inside atomic nuclei. And it turns outthere is a beautiful framework to encompass all these cases: Yang-Mills theory.

If you studied electromagnetism, you may remember that instead of manipulating the electric and magnetic fields, you can replace them with another field: the vector potential, often denoted A.

In 1954, Yang and Mills showed that we can generalize this idea to construct more theories than just electromagnetism. The field A now takes values in matrices, and the theory is described by a path integral and the following so-called Lagrangian:

L=−12g2Tr(FμνFμν),Fμν=∂μAν−∂νAμ−i[Aμ,Aν]\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2g^2}\,\mathrm{Tr}\left(F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}\right),
\qquad
F_{\mu\nu} = \partial_\mu A_\nu - \partial_\nu A_\mu - i\,[A_\mu, A_\nu]L=−2g21​Tr(Fμν​Fμν),Fμν​=∂μ​Aν​−∂ν​Aμ​−i[Aμ​,Aν​]

Here F plays the role of the electric and magnetic fields, g is the coupling constant, and[Aμ,Aν]=AμAν−AνAμ[A_\mu, A_\nu] = A_\mu A_\nu - A_\nu A_\mu[Aμ​,Aν​]=Aμ​Aν​−Aν​Aμ​is a commutator of matrices. Keep an eye on this last term: it will be the source of all theproblemsfun.

And what makes the idea powerful is thatthere is a free ingredient in this formulation: a group G. For all practical purposes, you can think of groups of matrices, like the unitary matrices of dimension N (the group U(N)) or the special unitary ones, with determinant 1 (the group SU(N)). When you write a Yang-Mills theory, you have to choose a group, and the field A takes values in the matrices associated with it.

If you pick U(1) (the "one-dimensional" unitary matrices, aka complex numbers of modulus 1), numbers commute, the commutator vanishes, and you get back electromagnetism. What about using other groups? If you use G=SU(2), you get the weak force (well... almost: you also need the Higgs field, but let's leave that aside...). Now if you choose G=SU(3), you get the strong nuclear force,a theory called Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD). That's why our best theory of particle physics, the so-called Standard Model, uses the "product" group G=U(1)×SU(2)×SU(3), which describesall three forces in a single framework. Add the matter particles (quarks, electrons and their cousins) and the Higgs field, and you get essentially everything we know about particle physics, except gravity. Beautiful, isn't it?

Well, actually, getting there wasn't that simple. Let's focus on Yang-Mills with G=SU(3), supposed to represent the strong nuclear force. This idea was initially met with skepticism (Wolfgang Pauli raised the objection...

articles.title: Silicon Valley claims to know the future. So why did it get the midterms so wrong?
articles.content: The self-styled visionaries of Silicon Valley, leaders like OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman and SpaceX boss Elon Musk, have built careers claiming to see the future. Long-term vision is currency: Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg built a 10-year road map for Facebook in 2016, and Google famously told investors before its public offering that it was unconcerned with short-term results. And yet there they all were, a mere five weeks before the midterm elections, gathered at the White House to smile for photos with President Trump and sign on to his “Super Intelligence” agenda. Even by the diminished standards of today’s corporate governance, this was a shockingly foolish decision. Despite dozens of polls showing a rising tide of anti-Trump sentiment and bipartisan rejection of AI and data centers, the futurists of the tech elite cast aside long-term corporate interests for short-term political favor. And now, their industry is very squarely in the new victors’ crosshairs. For an industry obsessed with pattern recognition, their decision to lash themselves to President Trump has proved to be a catastrophic misreading of the political landscape. Now, not only have they jeopardized their companies’ fates, but they’ve also raised questions about their vision and judgment.  What were they thinking? The people who work for them are just as confused as the rest of us. Tech workers I’ve spoken to at OpenAI, Meta, and other firms have noted an absence of commentary from their leaders post-election. Zuckerberg has yet to address the results internally, while an employee at another AI firm said that “leadership has been pretty silent on Slack.” Most employees share concern about potential anti-data-center legislation and are curious how leadership will adjust to a Democratic Washington, DC. But more than anything, they don’t understand how their bosses didn’t see what was so blindingly obvious to everyone else. In Silicon Valley, the Gretzkyism “skate to where the puck is going, not where it has been” is a management maxim; it preaches anticipation and foresight over reactiveness to the present moment. Tech entrepreneurs love a good “pivot,” and companies that can’t change with the times get disrupted and die. Which is why I find it so strange that Zuckerberg, OpenAI cofounder Greg Brockman, and so many of Silicon Valley’s other prominent AI leaders and venture capitalists have put themselves in a potentially inescapable political bind. In going all in on President Trump’s cultural and business agenda instead of playing both sides of the aisle as corporate America usually does, they’ve built identities they may not be able to pivot out of. Will anyone really believe that Palantir CEO Alex Karp is suddenly progressive after a year of promising “violence and death to our enemies” and telling investors that the company is “completely anti-woke”? I believe this is less a surprise than a very public exposure of a fundamental reality: that tech’s most visible leaders are not all-knowing visionary masterminds after all. Insights about social media or artificial intelligence do not make Zuckerberg or Altman experts on politics, the economy, or much else outside of technology. The instant gratification of presidential access, subsidies, and a say in their own regulation blinded them to the basics of political math that they clearly did not understand. There’s a reason the chief executives of Chase, Boeing, and other Fortune 500 staples don’t go on podcasts to talk about “masculine energy,” or call the president from the stage of a MAGA-friendly AI summit to label fears about AI a “hoax” and a “scam.” This is the learned wisdom of decades operating in an environment where the customer changes every four years but contracts run for 10. Most companies play to both sides of the aisle because they know that their business models and multibillion-dollar projects must outlast the current administration. Instead, Big Tech tied itself to Trump and made its most important goals and investments—many related to grid access and data center permits—immediate targets for Democrats. In tech, you can always sunset a feature or update some code. But in politics, there is no undo button for failures that change public perception. The tech elites’ decision to visibly align their businesses with a temporary movement has left them no credible way to pivot now that the climate has changed. As one Meta employee who has worked closely with Zuckerberg put it, “Mark is a long-term thinker, but he never charts a plan of how to get there. It’s spray and pray and see what happens.” As for whether employees expect the company to do a strategic postmortem? “Facebook has never really done that.” “Move fast and break things” might work in a startup, but it’s a terrible strategy for building reputational goodwill. Previous technological leaps, like the rollout of fiber-optic technology and wireless infrastructure, avoided partisan politics. But by kowtowing to the Trump administration, Silicon Valley made artificial intelligence a culture-war issue. Now, when citizens vote on data center proposals from California to Florida, they are no longer considering only technical or economic concerns, but political ones. Tech leaders didn’t see this coming because they were too focused on the urgency of the AI race to understand how reputational damage could undermine the intangible goodwill—and ultimately the very tangible infrastructure—necessary to win it. The industry’s misreading of the moment has already punctured one myth Silicon Valley holds dear: that its leaders can always see what’s next. Aaron Zamost is a tech communications consultant and a former executive at Square.
articles.summary: MIT 테크놀로지 리뷰의 논평은 주요 기술기업 지도자들이 트럼프 대통령의 ‘초지능’ 의제에 동참한 결정을 중간선거 이후의 정치적 위험과 연결해 비판한다. 글은 AI와 데이터센터에 대한 반감 속에서 기업들이 단기적인 정치적 호의를 장기적 이해관계보다 우선했다고 평가한다. 일부 기술기업 직원들은 데이터센터 반대 입법 가능성과 선거 이후 경영진의 대응 방향을 우려한다고 전한다. 이는 정책 환경에 관한 논평으로, 구체적인 규제 도입이나 사업상 손실이 확정됐다는 보도는 아니다.

articles.summary: 테크크런치는 젠슨 황이 사생활 관련 논란 이후 NVIDIA에서 사임했다고 전하며 사건의 흐름을 정리했다. 기사는 미국과 중국이 첨단 AI 인프라를 두고 경쟁하는 상황에서 이 사안이 국가안보에도 영향을 줄 가능성을 제기한다. 다만 제공된 발췌에는 구체적인 사건 경과나 안보상 영향의 근거가 없어, 이러한 파급효과는 가능성 수준으로 받아들여야 한다.
